newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asian Metals - China demand seen slack to 1997.
newsitem.headline: Asian Metals - China demand seen slack to 1997.

text.p: Far East base metals traders bemoaned on Monday a slowdown in business that they said was threatening to keep prices and demand weak at least until the Lunar Year of the Ox begins in February 1997.
Aluminium prices in China had fallen below domestic production costs, zinc prices would probably stay level on weak demand, lead was dead and copper confused, they said.

Even as London Metal Exchange aluminium prices drop -- with benchmark three-month futures touching a fresh 2-1/4 year low last Thursday of $1,340 from a peak the week before of $1,420 -- buyers had not jumped in, Asian traders said.
Buying would not begin until the market saw prices start to climb again, they added.
"China is not buying. I don't see people coming out and asking for 500 tonnes, 1,000 tonnes," an aluminium industry executive in Hong Kong said.

"Overall consumption has collapsed because of the property glut, which accounts for one-third of total consumption," he said, referring to an oversupply of residential and industrial real estate in China's boom areas, such as southern Guangdong.

Aluminium production for the whole of 1996 has been officially forecast at more than 1.8 million tonnes, 10 percent up on 1995's 1.65 million tonnes. The State Statistical Bureau reported aluminium output for the first eight months of 1996 was 1.0972 million tonnes, up 1.34 percent on the same 1995 period.
Imports of unwrought aluminium and aluminium materials in the first eight months of 1996 were 424,126 tonnes, up 13.6 percent on the year-ago period, customs figures show.

The Chinese official press warned at mid-year that aluminium supply was exceeding demand because of the year-on-year increases in imports. Much of the imported material was coming from Russia because it was cheap, the press reports.
Domestic prices were now around 13,000 yuan ($1,566) per tonne, traders said, down from 14,000 yuan just weeks ago.
Production cost per tonne was 15,000 yuan, said the Hong Kong source. "So they are already losing money,"
"They (aluminium producers) need cash flow because they have to keep paying their workers and paying off their loans, so they will probably still sell, even at 12,000 renminbi," he said.
South Korea and Japan had begun postponing shipments to use up existing stocks, traders said.

Chinese producers' inventories were also climbing, the Hong Kong executive said, adding there were unconfirmed rumours in the market that 40,000 tonnes of Russian material was sitting in warehouses at a northern Chinese port.
"If there is that much Russian material and unsold Chinese, it will overhang the market for six months," he said.
The rumours could not be independently confirmed.
The story was much the same for other base metal markets.
Zinc demand in Japan and South Korea "are both dead," a Chinese trader in Beijing said, though Taiwan and Southeast Asia remained firm.

China's biggest zinc smelter, the 330,000 tonne-per-annum Huludao plant in Liaoning province, had started up two months ago after closing for summer maintenance, he said. The plant was running at full capacity, producing 25,000 tonnes a month.

Huludao maintained a price advantage over other domestic producers by processing imported zinc concentrate for export. This avoided a 13 percent value-added tax on the imported material and an export tax of $50 a tonne.

Huludao zinc was now carrying a $40 premium for nearby prompt delivery, though Japanese orders for 1997, which were starting to come in from large users there, were carrying a $100 premium, the Chinese trader said.
China's largest nickel producer, Jinchuan Nonferrous, has already announced a $240 a tonne cut in its October sales price to try to push its product in a sluggish domestic market.
